companyCaseStudy.title: How GitHub Stopped Schema-Change Outages: gh-ost, Binlog Streaming, and Cutting Cutovers to <1s
companyCaseStudy.summary: ALTER TABLEs on huge MySQL tables used to be a site‑stopping operation at GitHub — minutes to hours of blocking writes and replication lag on a platform serving millions of Git operations. GitHub built gh-ost, an online schema migration tool, and moved migrations from risky maintenance windows to safe, automated, zero‑downtime operations (example: 300M‑row / 120GB table migrated online, cutover <1s).
companyCaseStudy.explanation:
## Hook: the schema-change boilover

At scale, schema changes are not innocent: a single ALTER TABLE can domino into minutes or hours of blocked writes, replication lag spikes, and customer-facing outages. GitHub — operating a global code hosting service with millions of repositories and high write rates — faced exactly that. They needed a way to change schemas on multi‑hundred‑million‑row tables without slowing down the site or scheduling big maintenance windows.

## Problem → Challenge

- Problem: ALTER TABLE on InnoDB tables often requires table rebuilds that lock or long‑block writes; slave replication lag spikes while a single large copy runs.
- Scale: GitHub runs MySQL clusters with tables hundreds of GBs and hundreds of millions of rows; Git operations generate high write throughput and wide distribution of traffic.
- Constraint: No acceptable downtime or prolonged performance regressions. Migrations had to be reversible, observable, and safe in the face of replication lag and failover.

Challenges included:
- Keeping the copy in sync while application writes keep changing rows.
- Avoiding spikes in replication lag on replicas during bulk copy.
- Making cutover atomic and fast (users cannot be routed away for minutes).
- Providing strong operational safety and the ability to throttle or abort.

## Solution: gh-ost (GitHub’s Online Schema Migration)

GitHub implemented gh-ost (open source) — a tool that performs online schema changes by streaming the MySQL binary log, copying data in small chunks, and doing a controlled cutover.

High-level flow:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
  AppWrites((App writes)) --> Master[(MySQL Master)]
  Master --> Replica[(Replica)]
  Master --> BinlogStreamer[gh-ost binlog streamer]
  BinlogStreamer --> GhostCopy[Ghost table (copy)]
  GhostCopy --> SyncState[Chunked copy + apply binlog diffs]
  SyncState --> Cutover[Atomic rename on master]
  Cutover --> Finished[Old table dropped / replica sync]
```

Key techniques used by gh-ost:
- Binlog streaming: gh-ost reads the master's binlog (or a replica's) and replays DML on the ghost table so the ghost remains up to date.
- Chunked copy: data is copied in small chunks (e.g., 1K–100K rows per chunk) with checks on replication lag and throttling to avoid impacting the master.
- Triggers only at cutover time: instead of heavy trigger usage, gh-ost uses binlog replay to avoid long‑standing triggers, minimizing overhead.
- Controlled cutover: once the ghost is in sync, gh-ost performs an atomic RENAME operation on the master that swaps the old table for the new one in a matter of milliseconds to seconds.
- Safety and observability: features include throttling based on replica lag, dry‑run mode, progress reporting, and an ability to abort and clean up.

### Architectural decisions and why they mattered

- Use binlog instead of long‑running triggers: avoids write amplification and long locks; binlog replay is efficient and decouples replication stream from copy.
- Chunked copying with lag-aware throttling: keeps replica lag under a threshold (e.g., <5s) and avoids causing traffic spikes or IO saturation.
- Atomic rename for cutover: RENAME TABLE on InnoDB is atomic and fast — no long table locks across the copy phase.
- Orchestration and automation: gh-ost can be run safely in CI/CD or by DBAs with strong logging and abort options.

## Results (real-world impact)

| Metric | Before (manual ALTER/Maintenance) | After (gh-ost online migration) |
|--------|-----------------------------------:|---------------------------------:|
| User-facing downtime for schema change | minutes → hours (blocking writes, outages) | ~0s (cutover measured in <1s–2s) |
| Replication lag spikes | large, unpredictable (tens of seconds to minutes) | controlled; kept under configured threshold (e.g., <5s)
| Risk of migration rollback | manual, error-prone | safe aborts and automatic cleanup
| Example migration (GitHub case) | N/A | 300M rows / ~120GB table copied online in ~8 hours; cutover <1s; zero downtime |

Notes: the example above reflects GitHub's operational experience: large tables (hundreds of millions of rows) were migrated online with no customer impact. Cutovers consistently complete in under a couple seconds because rename is atomic; total copy time depends on table size and DB throughput but can be throttled to avoid affecting live traffic.

## What changed operationally

- Migrations moved from 'maintenance windows' to regular ops — teams perform schema changes during normal deploys.
- Fewer emergency pages related to schema migration failures; incidents caused by schema changes dropped materially.
- DBAs gained more confidence: gh-ost provides safe defaults (replication lag checks, --max-load and --critical-load controls) and observability for long running jobs.

## Visual: migration lifecycle

```mermaid
graph LR
  subgraph CopyPhase
    A[Start copy] --> B[Copy chunk N]
    B --> C{Replication lag ok?}
    C -- yes --> B
    C -- no --> Throttle[Throttle / sleep]
    Throttle --> B
  end
  CopyPhase --> SyncPhase[Binlog replay catches up]
  SyncPhase --> CutoverPhase[Atomic RENAME on master]
  CutoverPhase --> Cleanup[Drop old table / finish]
```

## Tradeoffs and gotchas

- Copy time vs impact: copying a 100+GB table will still take hours; you trade off instant migration for background work that must be throttled to avoid impact.
- Requires binlog access and consistent replicas: gh-ost depends on a healthy replication topology and consistent binlogs.
- Not magic for all ALTERs: some operations (e.g., changing column type that requires on‑the‑fly transformation) need careful testing — gh-ost supports column transformations but operators must validate.

## Why this approach wins

- It preserves availability: the application continues to read/write while the migration is performed.
- It gives DBAs control: throttle, abort, and monitor; migrations become predictable.
- It leverages MySQL primitives (binlog, rename) for correctness and speed.

## TL;DR story arc

Problem: long, blocking ALTERs on multi‑hundred‑million row tables caused downtime and replication chaos.

Solution: gh-ost — binlog-driven, chunked copy + fast atomic rename + safety throttles.

Result: migrations of 100+GB tables done online with cutovers under a second, predictable replica lag, and far fewer schema-change incidents.
keyTakeaways: Use binlog streaming + chunked copy to keep a "ghost" table in sync — avoids long locks and triggers.
Make cutover atomic using RENAME TABLE; the heavy work happens in the background while live traffic continues.
Throttle based on replication lag and system load; safety and observability turn risky operations into routine ones.

concept.title: When Your API Starts Hiccuping: The Circuit Breaker Pattern for Resilient Services
concept.summary: Remote dependencies can fail or slow down — and when they do, naive retries or blocking calls can take your whole system down. The Circuit Breaker pattern prevents cascading failures by detecting errors and short‑circuiting calls, giving failing services time to recover while letting your system remain responsive.
keyTakeaways: Circuit breakers stop calling failing/slow dependencies to prevent cascading failures.
Use them together with timeouts, retries, bulkheads, and fallbacks for best results.
Tune thresholds and observe behaviour in production — wrong settings can cause flapping or silent failures.
